paragraphs.text: Challenger didn't simply 'explode': the external tank failed and aerodynamic forces tore the orbiter apart.
But that was only the visible part. The Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch. The key figure: 73 SECONDS.

To see why, look at the structure itself. Jan 27, 1986 night: Thiokol engineers argue against a cold launch; managers approve it. 11:38 EST: Liftoff; black smoke puffs from the right booster's aft joint. +59 s: A plume of flame appears at the joint. +73 s: External tank fails; Challenger breaks apart — 7 crew lost. Seventy-three seconds after launch, Challenger broke apart. Seven astronauts were killed, in front of the world. The cause was just a rubber ring, a quarter-inch thick. Overnight, temperatures fell well below freezing. Cold made the O-rings stiff, so they couldn't seal the booster joint. Burning gas escaped the joint and cut into the fuel tank. Engineers had warned against launching in the cold the night before. They were overruled. Today, that warning is taught to every engineer.
And the warning signs were already there. The mechanism: O-ring seal failure in a solid rocket booster field joint.

Then the chain began. The trigger: an O-ring seal stiffened by cold. Challenger didn't simply 'explode': the external tank failed and aerodynamic forces tore the orbiter apart. The crew cabin broke away largely intact.

This is the moment it could no longer be stopped. Step 1 of the failure chain: cold night below freezing. Step 2 of the failure chain: o-rINGS lose resilience. Step 3 of the failure chain: booster joint fails to seal. Step 4 of the failure chain: flame burns into external tank. Step 5 of the failure chain: VEHICLE BREAKS APART AT 73 s.
Which leaves one question. What changed: NASA redesigned the booster joints and changed how engineering objections are heard before launch.
But that was only the visible part. The engineers had the data but not the authority. If you were in that meeting the night before, how would you have made them listen?

miniNarrative: The Space Shuttle was a partially reusable spacecraft operated by the US National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA).
It flew for the first time in April 1981, and was used to conduct in-orbit research, and deploy commercial, military, and scientific payloads.
At launch, it consisted of the orbiter, which contained the crew and payload, the external tank (ET), and the two solid rocket boosters (SRBs).
The orbiter was a reusable, winged vehicle that launched vertically and landed as a glider.
